ncertReference.chapter: Section C: Structural Grammar, Tenses, Modals & Fill in the Blanks

thirtySecondSummary: Grammar Fill in the Blanks evaluates foundational structural rules: Subject-Verb Agreement, Verb Tense Sequences, Conditional Sentences, Modals, and Voice/Aspect.

Subject-Verb Agreement Core: Collective nouns (committee, jury) take singular verbs when acting as a unit, plural when divided; Indefinite pronouns like 'each', 'either', 'neither', 'everyone' strictly take singular verbs.

Conjunction Agreement: When subjects are joined by 'as well as', 'with', 'together with', 'along with', the verb agrees strictly with the FIRST subject; when joined by 'either... or' or 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the CLOSER (second) subject.
Conditionals: Type 1 (Real: If + Present, will + V1); Type 2 (Unreal Present: If + Past/were, would + V1); Type 3 (Unreal Past: If + had + V3, would have + V3).
Subjunctive Mood: Wishes and contrary-to-fact hypothetical statements use 'were' regardless of subject number (e.g., 'If I were the Prime Minister...').

coreConcepts.title: Subject-Verb Agreement: Advanced Governing Rules
coreConcepts.explanation:
The finite verb must agree with its true grammatical subject in person and number:
1. Parenthetical Phrases: Intervening phrases introduced by 'as well as', 'along with', 'accompanied by', 'together with', 'in addition to' do NOT change the number of the subject.
- Example: 'The captain, along with all his sailors, was (not were) rescued.'
2. Correlative Proximity Rule: When subjects are joined by 'either... or', 'neither... nor', or 'not only... but also', the verb agrees with the subject adjacent to it.
- Example: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were present.' vs 'Neither the students nor the teacher was present.'
3. Indefinite Pronouns: 'Each', 'every', 'everyone', 'everybody', 'anyone', 'nobody', 'either', 'neither', 'one of the...' strictly govern singular verbs.
- Example: 'Each of the participants has (not have) submitted the project.'
- 'One of the students who have passed' (Here, 'who' refers to plural 'students', hence 'have').
keyTakeaways: 'Along with', 'as well as' -> Verb agrees with Subject 1.
'Neither... nor' -> Verb agrees with nearest Subject 2.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: CBSE Class XII Core English, Subject-Verb Concord, pp. 240-254.

coreConcepts.title: The Three Canonical Conditional Constructions
coreConcepts.explanation:
Conditional sentences express conditions and their contingent outcomes:
1. Zero Conditional (Universal Truths / Scientific Facts):
- Formula: If + Simple Present, ... Simple Present.
- E.g.: 'If you heat ice, it melts.'
2. Type 1 Conditional (Probable / Real Future):
- Formula: If + Simple Present (V1), ... will / can / may + Base Verb (V1).
- E.g.: 'If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the excursion.'
3. Type 2 Conditional (Hypothetical / Unreal Present):
- Formula: If + Simple Past (V2 / were), ... would / could + Base Verb (V1).
- E.g.: 'If I knew his address, I would write to him.' / 'If I were you, I would accept the scholarship.'
4. Type 3 Conditional (Unreal Past / Past Counterfactual):
- Formula: If + Past Perfect (had + V3), ... would have + Past Participle (V3).
- E.g.: 'If you had studied diligently, you would have cleared the examination.' (Inversion: 'Had you studied diligently, you would have cleared...').
keyTakeaways: Type 3: If + had + V3, would have + V3.
Inversion form: 'Had he known...' = 'If he had known...'.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: CUET English Grammar Guide, Conditional Clauses & Inversion, pp. 256-265.

coreConcepts.title: Tense Sequences and Time Anchor Rules
coreConcepts.explanation:
1. Sequence of Tenses: When the principal clause verb is in the past tense, subordinate clause verbs must be in the past tense (Exception: Universal truths e.g., 'The teacher said that the Earth revolves around the Sun').
2. 'Since' as a Time Anchor: When 'since' introduces a specific starting point in time, the main clause requires the Present Perfect tense, while the 'since' clause uses Simple Past.
- Formula: Present Perfect + since + Simple Past.
- E.g.: 'Five years have elapsed since he graduated from university.'
3. By the Time / Future Perfect: An action that will be completed prior to a designated point in the future uses Future Perfect.
- Formula: By the time + Simple Present, ... will have + V3.
- E.g.: 'By the time the train arrives, we will have bought the tickets.'
keyTakeaways: Main clause Past -> Subordinate Past (unless universal truth).
Present Perfect + since + Simple Past ('I have not seen him since he left').
Future Perfect: 'will have + V3' coupled with 'by next year' or 'by the time'.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: NTA CUET English Language Practice Tests, Tenses & Verb Patterns, pp. 266-275.

keyFacts.concept: The 'One of the + Plural Noun + Who + Plural Verb' Rule
keyFacts.formulaOrFact: One of the [Plural Noun] who [Plural Verb]
keyFacts.explanation: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural antecedent noun immediately preceding it, requiring a plural verb.
keyFacts.examTip: 'He is one of the scholars who have (not has) shaped modern history.'

keyFacts.formulaOrFact: If + Subject + were ... (Regardless of singular/plural subject)
keyFacts.examTip: 'If I were a bird' (Never 'If I was a bird' in formal CUET English).

keyFacts.formulaOrFact: 'Lest' must be followed by 'should' (or bare subjunctive verb)
keyFacts.explanation: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and inherently contains a negative meaning, so 'not' must NEVER be used after it.
keyFacts.examTip: 'Walk carefully lest you should fall' (Never 'lest you should not fall').

workedExamples.question:
Fill in the blank with the grammatically correct option:
'The commanding general, along with several high-ranking officers, ________ inspecting the frontier defense positions when the skirmish erupted.'
solutionSteps: Step 1: Identify the true grammatical subject: 'The commanding general' (Singular, 3rd person).
Step 2: Note the parenthetical connective: 'along with several high-ranking officers'. Phrases introduced by 'along with' do not pluralize the singular head noun.
Step 3: Past continuous context: 'when the skirmish erupted' requires past tense.
Step 4: Singular past auxiliary = 'was'. Option B is correct.
workedExamples.cuetInsight: Parenthetical phrases (along with, as well as, together with) are standard subject-verb agreement test traps.

workedExamples.question:
Complete the conditional sentence correctly:
'If the rescue team ________ thirty minutes earlier, they ________ the trapped mountaineers before the blizzard struck.'
solutionSteps: Step 1: Analyze the time frame: The event refers to an unfulfilled condition in the past (Type 3 conditional).
Step 2: Formula for Type 3: If + Past Perfect (had + V3) ... would have + Past Participle (would have + V3).
Step 3: If the rescue team 'had arrived' ... they 'would have saved'. Option B fits the rule perfectly.
workedExamples.cuetInsight: Remember that 'would have' NEVER appears in the 'if'-clause itself (e.g., 'If they would have arrived' is a fatal grammatical error).

howCuetAsks.typicalStem: Each of the scientific instruments in the laboratory ________ calibrated weekly.
howCuetAsks.strategy: 'Each of' is strictly singular -> 'is calibrated' / 'has been calibrated'.

howCuetAsks.typicalStem: Had the warning been issued in time, the villagers ________ evacuated.
howCuetAsks.strategy: Inversion of Type 3 ('Had + V3') requires 'would have been' in the main clause.

commonTraps.whyItTraps: People say colloquially 'If I would have known', which is strictly ungrammatical in formal English.
commonTraps.howToAvoid: 'If' takes 'had + V3'; 'would have' belongs exclusively to the main clause.

commonTraps.whyItTraps: Two people are involved, so students choose a plural verb ('Neither of the boys were present').
commonTraps.howToAvoid: 'Neither of' means 'not one of the two' and is strictly singular ('was present').

mnemonics.meaning: Type 3 conditionals always match 'had' in the if-clause with 'would have' in the result clause.
mnemonics.application: Instant verification of Type 3 conditional grammar.

quickRevisionCard.title: Grammar & Fill in the Blanks Summary
keyPoints: As well as / Along with: Verb agrees strictly with Subject 1.
Either... or / Neither... nor: Verb agrees with Subject 2 (closer subject).
Each / Every / Neither of / Either of: Strictly singular verbs.
Type 1: If + V1, will + V1 | Type 2: If + V2/were, would + V1 | Type 3: If + had + V3, would have + V3.
Subjunctive: 'If I were...' (never 'was' in hypothetical conditions).
Lest: Must be followed by 'should' without 'not'.
Since Rule: Present Perfect + since + Simple Past ('I have lived here since 2015').

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank with the correct verb form:
'Neither the principal nor the teachers ________ present at the emergency staff meeting yesterday.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: When subjects are joined by 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the closer subject ('the teachers', plural), and 'yesterday' requires past tense ('were').

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank:
'Walk briskly, lest you ________ miss the last suburban train.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: The conjunction 'lest' (meaning 'for fear that') grammatically requires the modal auxiliary 'should'.

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank:
'Dr. Radhakrishnan is one of those eminent philosophers who ________ contributed profoundly to East-West cultural understanding.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: In 'one of those [Plural Noun] who...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural antecedent 'philosophers', requiring the plural verb 'have'.

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements:
Assertion (A): The sentence 'If I was the President of the country, I would abolish this tax' contains a grammatical error.
Reason (R): In formal English, hypothetical or contrary-to-fact conditional clauses require the subjunctive mood verb 'were' regardless of whether the subject is singular or plural.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

practiceQuestions.explanation: Both statements are completely true and (R) explains the subjunctive rule requiring 'If I were...' rather than 'If I was...'.

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank:
'Ten years ________ elapsed since the historic peace accord was signed in Geneva.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ten discrete individual years passing one by one takes the plural verb 'have elapsed' in conjunction with the 'since' clause.

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank:
'Had the driver seen the red signal in time, the accident ________.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: 'Had the driver seen...' is an inverted Type 3 conditional, requiring 'would have been avoided' in the passive main clause.

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank:
'The jury ________ divided in their opinions regarding the culpability of the accused.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: When members of a collective noun act individually or are divided in opinion (signaled by 'divided' and 'their'), the collective noun takes a plural verb ('were').

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank:
'By this time next year, my sister ________ her doctorate degree in astrophysics.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: Actions that will be completed by a designated future deadline ('by this time next year') require the Future Perfect tense ('will have completed').

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank:
'Neither of the two candidates who contested the parliamentary by-election ________ able to secure a majority.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb ('was able') because it means 'not one of the two'.

practiceQuestions.question:
Fill in the blank with the appropriate preposition:
'The company's practices are not in compliance ________ the latest environmental safety regulations.'
practiceQuestions.explanation: 'In compliance with' is the fixed grammatical idiom in English.
